platforms.title: Why That Red Patch in Your Eye Isn't As Scary As It Looks
platforms.meta_description: A sudden red patch in the white of your eye looks alarming, but a subconjunctival hemorrhage is almost always harmless and heals on its own, per Mayo Clinic.
platforms.body_html:
Catching a glimpse in the mirror of a bright red patch spreading across the white of your eye is genuinely startling. Most of the time, though, this is something called a subconjunctival hemorrhage — and despite how it looks, it's rarely something to worry about.

Why the White of Your Eye Turns Red

Just beneath the conjunctiva, the thin clear membrane covering the white of the eye, run some extremely delicate blood vessels. When one of them breaks, the blood pooling underneath shows through the conjunctiva, turning the whole area bright red. Mayo Clinic explains that this can happen from coughing, sneezing, rubbing your eyes hard, or sometimes for no identifiable reason at all. The vessels themselves are so thin and fragile that even a small, brief, momentary spike in pressure can be more than enough to rupture one of them entirely.

What matters most is what else is going on. A subconjunctival hemorrhage typically causes no pain, no vision changes, and no discharge — the redness is essentially the only symptom, aside from possible mild irritation. According to Mayo Clinic, it usually clears up on its own within one to three weeks without any treatment, absorbing back into the tissue the same way a bruise on your skin gradually fades over time.

When You Should Actually See a Doctor

That said, not every case is safe to simply wait out. First, if the redness appeared after a hard hit to the eye or a significant blow to the head, get it checked right away. Second, if pain, light sensitivity, or blurred vision shows up alongside the redness, it may not be a simple subconjunctival hemorrhage at all. Third, if the red patch hasn't started fading after two to three weeks, or these hemorrhages keep happening repeatedly, it's worth having a doctor check for an underlying blood or blood pressure issue.

It's easy to confuse a subconjunctival hemorrhage with conjunctivitis, or pink eye. Conjunctivitis usually comes with discharge, itchiness, and redness spread evenly across the eye that doesn't fade quickly. A subconjunctival hemorrhage, by contrast, tends to show up as a sharply defined patch of solid red in one spot, with no itching or discharge, and it only fades gradually over time rather than changing much day to day. Knowing that difference makes it much easier to decide whether to see a doctor or simply keep an eye on it.

Day to day, artificial tears for any dryness or irritation are usually all you need, along with avoiding rubbing the eye and skipping contact lenses until the redness clears. If these episodes keep recurring, it's worth reviewing your medications too — blood thinners like aspirin and warfarin are recognized risk factors for subconjunctival hemorrhage, and uncontrolled high blood pressure is known to weaken small vessel walls the same way. If any one of those three warning signs applies to you, don't just wait it out on your own — get it properly checked and looked at by an eye doctor instead.
